story_title: 55 Years of American Driving: Miles Traveled vs. Gas Prices
story_subtitle: From 1956 to 2010, watch how the nation’s appetite for the road collided with volatile pump prices—and see which way the needle really moved.

story_pieces.narration: Between 1956 and 1973, vehicle-miles climbed steadily from 3 675 B to 6 154 B while gas prices drifted down from $2.38 to $1.90 per gallon (2021-corrected dollars), creating a classic cheap-fuel boom that rewarded every extra mile.
story_pieces.question: How did the long cheap-fuel era shape America’s driving habit up to the first oil shock?
story_pieces.visualization: bar chart race of annual miles with overlaid price line

story_pieces.narration: The 1973-74 embargo flipped the script: miles dropped 3.4 % in 1974 and prices spiked 23 % to $2.34—still the fastest single-year cost jump in the series—revealing immediate elasticity once pain at the pump arrived.
story_pieces.question: What happened to driving distance and price the moment oil-supply security cracked?
story_pieces.visualization: combo slope chart (1973 vs 1974) with miles bar and price dot

story_pieces.narration: From 1978 to 1981, miles inched up only 4 % while gas rocketed from $2.23 to $3.30, producing the steepest price-to-miles ratio (3.2×) of any three-year window and marking the first sustained conservation period.
story_pieces.question: Did the second oil crisis finally force Americans to curb mileage growth?
story_pieces.visualization: scatter plot with 1978-81 highlighted path showing price vs miles

story_pieces.narration: After 1986’s price collapse to $1.76, miles resumed growth; yet sharp price spikes in 2005 and 2008 again trimmed mileage—2008’s $3.31 peak coincided with a rare year-over-year decline, proving price sensitivity never went away.
story_pieces.question: Does driving still react to price spikes once memories of crisis fade?

story_pieces.narration: Over the full 55-year span, cumulative miles expanded 2.7× while real gas prices rose only 10 %, yielding an almost vertical long-run supply curve—implying that, barring acute shocks, Americans choose mobility almost regardless of gradual price creep.
story_pieces.question: In the very long run, did higher gas prices meaningfully slow the growth of driving?
story_pieces.visualization: semi-log line chart (log miles vs linear price) with trend-break annotations
